About NITIZEN

Built for the Citizen Nigeria Deserves

NITIZEN fuses “Nigeria” with “citizen” — a deliberate declaration that active, informed citizenship is the foundation of the country we want to build.

Nigeria is at a crossroads. With a median age of under 20, its population is overwhelmingly youthful — yet civic participation, policy literacy, and democratic engagement remain dangerously low. NITIZEN is built to change that.

We are not a passive audience to governance; we are its architects, its critics, its conscience. Through AI-assisted civic learning, editorial analysis, civic reporting, institutional tracking, and creative community engagement — NITIZEN creates a digital environment where citizens don’t just consume information. They act on it.

Our immediate focus is the 2027 general elections: preparing citizens to vote with clarity, purpose, and accountability. The mission extends beyond any single cycle — NITIZEN is long-term civic infrastructure.

🎯 Our Mission

To equip Nigerians — especially youth — with knowledge, critical thinking, and participatory channels for active democratic engagement.

🌍 Our Vision

A Nigeria where every citizen — regardless of class, geography, or education — can engage with political power, hold leadership accountable, and shape national decisions.

⚙️ Our Approach

Technology, media, and storytelling combined — AI, multimedia criticism, and long-form civic writing in a single platform accessible to every Nigerian with a smartphone.

📍 Our Context

Policy & Advocacy, Electoral Engagement, Accountability & Transparency, Social Inclusion — the thematic pillars of good governance for Nigeria.

Citizens finding their civic voice — the NITIZEN mission made visible

How NITIZEN Speaks to Nigeria’s Moment

Policy & Advocacy

Conscience Letters situates every policy decision within historical and ethical context, empowering citizens to advocate from knowledge rather than frustration.

Electoral Engagement

With 2027 in view, NITIZEN deploys electoral literacy campaigns, candidate-assessment tools, and voter mobilisation resources across all 36 states.

Accountability & Transparency

Critika's creative accountability framework and AskNaija's data-backed responses create twin pillars of public oversight — one artistic, one analytical.

Social Inclusion

Designed for non-elite audiences — rural youth, women, the economically excluded — NITIZEN ensures civic power isn’t only for the already-powerful.

National Cohesion & Peace

By fostering shared civic identity rooted in common rights and responsibilities rather than ethnic division, NITIZEN builds the connective tissue of a unified Nigeria.

Technology as Social Change

AI, digital storytelling, and multimedia are core delivery mechanisms for civic intelligence here — not decorative features, but structural tools for scale.

Three Pillars.

NITIZEN is structured around three interlocking initiatives — each targeting a different dimension of the civic education gap, designed to scale through technology, community, and creativity.

INITIATIVE 01
Conscience Letters

"The record that refuses to fade."

NITIZEN's long-form editorial home — rigorous, evidence-based civic writing holding leadership accountable to the documented record. Editorially independent, permanently archived, and written so that 2027 does not repeat what history already proved preventable.

Flagship Objective: Establish Nigeria's most credible civic editorial canon — a permanent, citable record of governance performance that shapes public memory and 2027 electoral judgment.

UNIQUE MANDATE: ANALYSIS, HISTORY, AND ACCOUNTABILITY JOURNALISM. THE ONLY PLATFORM WHERE EDITORIAL RIGOUR MEETS CIVIC PURPOSE.

AskNaija

Nigeria's AI-powered civic intelligence tool — live in Phase 2 Beta. AskNaija answers questions on governance, elections, policy, and rights with sourced, contextual responses, bridging the information gap that keeps ordinary citizens disengaged from democratic participation.

UNIQUE MANDATE: AI-POWERED CIVIC INTELLIGENCE. NO EDITORIALISING — PURE, SOURCED INFORMATION DELIVERY AT SCALE.

STRATEGIC VALUE: SCALES CIVIC EDUCATION BEYOND WHAT HUMAN WRITERS CAN PRODUCE — ONE AI TOOL REACHING MILLIONS SIMULTANEOUSLY.

See-gnal

"Nigeria sees. Nigeria speaks. Nothing is erased."

The civic accountability and community action platform — four distinct channels for citizen participation: RedFlag (report abuse and injustice), The Ledger (track sector performance with data), OpenMic (testimony and civil discourse), and Critika (accountability through art and creativity).

Flagship Objective: Create Nigeria's most comprehensive citizen-powered accountability archive — a permanent, public, searchable record of governance failures, civic data, and community testimony.

Why It Matters

The Civic Gap We Are Closing

Nigeria faces a deepening civic participation crisis. Despite being home to over 100 million young people, youth engagement with governance structures remains critically low. Voter apathy, policy illiteracy, and disengagement from democratic processes are widespread.

Most Nigerians cannot readily obtain clear answers about how government works, what their rights are, or how to hold leadership accountable. NITIZEN exists to close that gap — permanently — through three purposefully designed civic tools.

NTZ·CL·001 — Conscience Letters · Governance · Economy · NITIZEN Editorial · May 2026
Governance · Economy · Conscience Letters No. 001

The Promise and the Price: What Tinubu's Subsidy Removal Means for the Nigerian Poor

NITIZEN EDITORIAL · MAY 2026 · 8 MIN READ

When President Bola Tinubu stepped onto the podium at Eagle Square on May 29, 2023, and declared that "fuel subsidy is gone," the crowd erupted. For many Nigerians — particularly the elite commentariat and economic reform advocates — it was the sound of a long-overdue reckoning. The subsidy, they argued, had for decades been a drain on the public treasury: a leaking pipe that cost the government trillions of naira annually while disproportionately benefiting the wealthy who owned multiple cars and the fuel importers who had turned the system into a private ATM.

They were not entirely wrong. The fuel subsidy regime was ridden with corruption, opacity, and inefficiency. The NNPCL's books were a maze. The subsidy verification processes were susceptible to manipulation. Billions disappeared into a system that was, at its worst, a sophisticated mechanism for transferring public wealth into private hands.

But economic arguments, however valid, do not exist in a vacuum. They exist in the real conditions of real people — and the real conditions of Nigeria are these: over 100 million citizens living below the poverty line[¹]; a minimum wage that had not been meaningfully reviewed in years; a naira in freefall; and an inflation rate that climbed to 28.92% by December 2023[²] — and would continue rising to a peak of 34.8% by February 2024 — the highest levels recorded since Nigeria began tracking CPI inflation in its current form.

"When you remove a subsidy in a country with no social safety net, no functioning public transportation, and a collapsed manufacturing sector, you are not reforming an economy. You are conducting an experiment on the poor."

The Arithmetic of Suffering

Let us be precise about what happened. Before May 29, 2023, Nigerians purchased petrol at approximately ₦185 per litre.[³] Verified Within weeks of the subsidy removal, the pump price had climbed to over ₦600 per litre. Verified By 2025, it crossed ₦1,000 in many parts of the country. For a bus driver in Aba, a petty trader in Maiduguri, a bricklayer in Kaduna — this was not a policy reform. It was an economic catastrophe visited upon them without warning, without cushion, and without a plan.

Transportation costs doubled, then tripled. The price of food — overwhelmingly transported by road across Nigeria's vast geography — rose in lockstep. The cost of running generators, which millions of Nigerians depend on because the national grid delivers on average fewer than eight hours of electricity daily[⁴], became unbearable for households already stretched to breaking point.

The government promised palliatives. They came late, were poorly targeted, and were widely regarded as inadequate. A one-time payment of ₦8,000 to the poorest Nigerians[⁵] Verified — the figure that circulated in early government communications — was widely mocked. For context: ₦8,000 would not cover a week's transportation costs for a Lagos market woman at the new petrol prices.

The Moral Question

This piece is not an argument for the return of the fuel subsidy. It is an argument about how reform is conducted — and who bears its cost. Economic reform that places its entire burden on those least equipped to absorb it is not courage. It is negligence dressed in the language of progress.

The Tinubu administration had options. A phased removal could have given households and businesses time to adjust. Direct and verifiable cash transfers to the most vulnerable — managed transparently — could have cushioned the blow. Investment in public transportation infrastructure, in parallel with subsidy removal, would have created an alternative to private vehicle dependence. None of these were in place when the subsidy was yanked away on inauguration day.

The price of that unpreparedness has been paid — is being paid — by the Nigerian poor. This is the record. And a democracy worthy of the name demands that we read it clearly.

References & Sources
  • [¹]World Bank Nigeria Poverty Assessment 2022 — "Nigeria's poverty headcount ratio at $2.15/day (2017 PPP) was 40.1% (c. 2018–19), with projections exceeding 100 million persons in absolute terms by 2024 given inflation trajectory." worldbank.org/en/country/nigeria
  • [²]National Bureau of Statistics (NBS), Consumer Price Index Reports. Headline inflation December 2023: 28.92%. Headline inflation February 2024: 34.8% (peak after CPI rebasing). NBS CPI Rebasing Report, January 2024. nigeriastat.gov.ng
  • [³]NNPC Petroleum Products Pricing Regulatory Agency (PPPRA), Historical Pump Price Data. Pre-May 2023 official regulated pump price: ₦185/litre. Corroborated by Premium Times, Punch, and Vanguard reporting, May 2023.
  • [⁴]Transmission Company of Nigeria (TCN), National Grid Situation Reports 2023–2024. Average daily generation: 4,000–5,000MW; distribution losses reduce effective supply to under 8hrs in many zones. tcn.org.ng
  • [⁵]Federal Ministry of Humanitarian Affairs, National Social Safety Nets Coordinating Office (NASSCO) — Subsidy Palliative Communications, June–August 2023. ₦8,000 per household disbursement figure reported by The Cable, Punch, and NAN (News Agency of Nigeria), June 2023.

This piece represents the editorial position of NITIZEN's Conscience Letters initiative. We welcome responses and counter-arguments at hello@nitizen.ng. Conscience Letters is committed to evidence-based civic analysis and welcomes diverse perspectives.

NTZ·CL·004 — Conscience Letters · Electoral Democracy · NITIZEN Editorial · June 2026
Electoral Democracy · Conscience Letters No. 004

The Ballot and the Broken Promise: Nigeria's Electoral History and What 2027 Must Learn From It

NITIZEN EDITORIAL · JUNE 2026 · 10 MIN READ

The Independent National Electoral Commission carries a name that, for many Nigerians, has become ironic. "Independent" — from what, exactly? The INEC that conducted the 2023 general elections oversaw a process that generated more litigation, more controversy, and more citizen outrage than arguably any election in Nigeria's Fourth Republic history. The Supreme Court eventually upheld the presidential result.[¹] Verified But a court's verdict on the legality of a process is not the same as a citizenry's confidence in its integrity.

As the country turns its attention toward 2027, the integrity of the electoral process is not merely a procedural question. It is the central question of Nigerian democracy. An election that citizens do not trust — regardless of its technical outcomes — corrodes the legitimacy of governance and deepens the disengagement that already plagues the republic.

"An election that citizens do not trust is not a democracy functioning. It is a democracy performing."

But to understand where we are, we must understand where we have been. Nigeria's electoral history is not a story of steady progress. It is a story of cycles — of promise, manipulation, crisis, and partial recovery — repeated with enough variation to discourage hope and enough resilience to refuse extinction.

The First Republic and the Original Sin (1959–1966)

Nigeria's first federal election under universal suffrage, held in December 1959, was in many ways a colonial handover exercise. The three dominant parties — the NPC in the north, the NCNC in the east, and the Action Group in the west — contested along lines that mirrored the country's regional and ethnic divisions far more than any coherent ideological differentiation. The NPC, dominant in the more populous north, emerged with the most seats and formed a coalition government with the NCNC under Sir Abubakar Tafawa Balewa as Prime Minister.[²]

What followed was the foundational lesson Nigeria has never fully absorbed: that electoral competition in a multi-ethnic, multi-religious polity without strong civic institutions and independent adjudication is a recipe not for democratic consolidation but for zero-sum warfare. The 1964–65 federal and regional elections descended into violence, rigging, and boycotts of a scale that shocked even seasoned colonial administrators. The Western Region crisis of 1965 — in which election results were so brazenly manipulated that rival politicians declared parallel victories — set the conditions for the first military coup of January 15, 1966.[²] Nigeria's first experiment with democracy lasted six years. It was killed not by an external enemy but by the failure of its own political class to respect the verdict of the ballot.

Military Interruptions and Managed Transitions (1966–1999)

The thirty-three years between the first coup and 1999 were a democratic graveyard. Gowon promised transition and delivered civil war. Obasanjo's first administration produced the credible Second Republic handover of 1979 — only for Buhari's coup in December 1983 to terminate it, citing the same rigging the political class had perfected.[³] Babangida's eight-year rule then produced the most consequential election in Nigerian history: June 12, 1993, won decisively by MKO Abiola and annulled by the same Babangida who had commissioned it. That annulment remains the deepest wound in Nigeria's democratic memory — proof that Nigerians could vote across ethnic lines when given the chance, and that the military would not accept results threatening its institutional interests. Abiola's death in detention in 1998, and Abacha's intervening dictatorship, marked the moral nadir of Nigerian governance. Abdulsalami Abubakar's compressed transition eventually produced Obasanjo's election as president in February 1999.[³]

The Fourth Republic: Patterns of Partial Democracy (1999–2015)

The elections of 1999 returned Nigeria to civilian rule, but they did not return it to democratic integrity. The 2003 elections, conducted by INEC under Justice Abel Guobadia, were widely criticised for rigging, violence, and result fabrication on a scale that dwarfed anything in the post-1999 period.[⁴] Obasanjo's reelection was secured through a process that domestic observers, the EU Election Observation Mission, and civil society groups described in unambiguous terms. "Massaged results" was the diplomatic phrasing; "stolen" was the more honest one.

The 2007 elections — transitioning power to Umaru Musa Yar'Adua — were arguably worse. INEC under Maurice Iwu presided over a process that the EU observation mission described as falling "far short of basic international and regional standards."[⁴] Yar'Adua himself, in his inauguration speech, acknowledged the "imperfections" of the election that brought him to power — a remarkable admission that became a statement of intent when his administration initiated the 2008 Electoral Reform Committee under Justice Muhammadu Uwais.

The Uwais Report's recommendations were substantially diluted by the National Assembly. What emerged was partial reform: enough to make 2011 significantly more credible under Attahiru Jega, but not enough to close the structural gaps that enable manipulation. Even the 2011 elections produced post-election violence in twelve northern states that killed over 800 people[⁴] — a reminder that credibility and stability are not the same thing.

2015: The Pivot That Was and Wasn't

The 2015 general elections were, by measurable standards, a genuine turning point. For the first time in Nigerian history, an incumbent president — Goodluck Jonathan — conceded defeat and congratulated his opponent before the formal announcement of results.[⁵] Muhammadu Buhari's victory under the All Progressives Congress marked the first democratic transfer of power between parties in Nigeria's history. The international community celebrated. Nigerians — many of them — wept with relief. It felt, for a moment, like the June 12 wound might finally heal.

The moment deserved that optimism. What followed tested it. The 2019 elections, also conducted under Buhari, were marred by voter suppression, violence — particularly in Rivers State — and widespread allegations of result manipulation. INEC's credibility, rebuilt under Jega, began to erode again under Mahmood Yakubu. The passage of the Electoral Act 2022 — which introduced the provision for electronic transmission of results and the use of BVAS — represented genuine legislative progress.[⁵] But legislation is only as strong as the institution mandated to implement it.

What Went Wrong in 2023

The 2023 presidential election was, by INEC's own design, supposed to be its most transparent ever. The Bimodal Voter Accreditation System (BVAS) was introduced to prevent the manipulation of voter accreditation.[⁶] The INEC Result Viewing Portal (IReV) was launched with the promise of real-time upload of polling unit results — a measure designed to make result falsification visible and traceable.

Both innovations failed, or were failed, at critical moments. The IReV portal experienced what INEC described as technical difficulties during the critical early hours of result transmission. Many results appeared hours or days late. Discrepancies between polling unit results and collated figures were documented by domestic and international observers. INEC's own officials were arraigned in some states for alleged electoral malpractice. Verified[⁷]

The three-way contest between Tinubu (APC), Atiku Abubakar (PDP), and Peter Obi (Labour Party) added a dimension Nigeria had not seen in the Fourth Republic: a genuinely competitive third-party candidate drawing massive youth support, the so-called "Obidient" movement, which demonstrated that Nigerian voters — particularly younger ones — were capable of refusing the binary between established parties. Obi's 25.7% of the presidential vote represented the strongest third-party performance since 1979. The movement's energy was real. Its structural limitations — lack of ground infrastructure, party machinery, and legislative presence — were equally real.

The Supreme Court upheld Tinubu's election on February 6, 2024.[¹] The ruling resolved the legal question. It did not resolve the credibility question. And in a democracy, both matter — because one is about the law, and the other is about the people who live under it.

The Lessons History Has Already Taught Us

Six decades of electoral experience have produced a set of lessons that Nigeria's political class has studied carefully — and applied, in many cases, for the purpose of subverting rather than strengthening democracy. For citizens, those same lessons are instruction manuals for civic vigilance:

Lesson One: Ethnic and regional arithmetic does not determine — but does constrain — electoral outcomes. From 1959 to 2023, the dominant pattern has been coalition-building along ethnic and regional lines. But 1993 and 2015 demonstrated that when civic conditions allow genuine choice, Nigerians vote across those lines. The pattern is not destiny. It is a habit — and habits can be broken by a sufficiently motivated citizenry.

Lesson Two: Institutional independence is everything. Every credible election Nigeria has conducted — 1979, 1993, 2011, 2015 — was overseen by an electoral commission that had, or was perceived to have, some degree of genuine independence from incumbent power. Every deeply discredited election involved an INEC (or its predecessors) compromised by executive influence, inadequate resourcing, or institutional cowardice. The appointment process, funding independence, and security of tenure of electoral commissioners are not administrative details. They are the architecture of democratic legitimacy.

Lesson Three: Technology is a tool, not a solution. BVAS and IReV in 2023 were theoretically sound innovations. They were not sufficiently protected from institutional failure, network unreliability, or the human decisions made at collation centres. Electronic systems amplify integrity when the surrounding institution has integrity. When that condition is absent, they amplify the appearance of transparency while enabling the reality of manipulation.

Lesson Four: Civic participation determines the cost of rigging. In every well-documented instance of electoral fraud in Nigeria, the fraud has been easier where voter apathy was highest. Large turnouts, active polling unit monitors, and a citizenry that knows its rights and acts on them raise the cost of manipulation to the point where it becomes operationally difficult. This is not idealism. It is the documented mechanics of election security.

Lesson Five: The absence of a PVC is a vote for whoever wins. Nigeria's voter registration is not automatic. It requires deliberate action. In 2023, an estimated 9.4 million registered voters did not collect their Permanent Voter Cards.[⁸] Those voters were registered in the system but effectively disenfranchised — not by anyone else's action, but by their own inaction. In a country where elections have been decided by margins of hundreds of thousands of votes, uncollected PVCs are not a bureaucratic oversight. They are an electoral catastrophe.

The Road to 2027: What Must Change

What must change before 2027 to restore citizen confidence? Three things, at minimum: transparent technology, independent oversight, and civic preparedness.

On technology: INEC must not only deploy electronic systems but must demonstrate, through pre-election public testing and open-source verification, that those systems are tamper-resistant and reliably connected. The failure of IReV in 2023 cannot be excused a second time. As of May 2026, INEC has signalled plans for a new voter register update exercise and improvements to its results transmission infrastructure. Citizens must demand proof, not promises.

On oversight: The composition of INEC's leadership and its appointment process must be revisited. An electoral commission whose chair is appointed solely by the executive, without meaningful legislative or civil society oversight, cannot credibly claim independence. Electoral reform legislation that restructures this dynamic is not a luxury — it is the minimum requirement for a credible 2027 election. Civil society organisations, including the Transition Monitoring Group, YIAGA Africa, and the Centre for Democracy and Development, have been consistent advocates for this reform. Their work deserves amplification and active citizen support.

On civic preparedness: this is where citizens hold power that no institution can take from them — if they choose to exercise it.

Where NITIZEN Stands in This Landscape

Nigeria has no shortage of electoral commentary. It has a critical shortage of structured, permanently available civic intelligence — the kind that survives election cycles, requires no university degree to use, and serves no party or sponsor. NITIZEN was built for that gap. Conscience Letters provides the historical and analytical record. AskNaija answers specific questions on voter registration, polling procedures, and rights with sourced, verifiable information. See-gnal provides citizen documentation infrastructure — RedFlag for reporting irregularities, The Ledger for institutional tracking, OpenMic for testimony, Critika for creative accountability. Together they form something Nigeria has not had: a permanent civic infrastructure accountable to citizens. NITIZEN's role in 2027 is not to tell Nigerians how to vote. It is to ensure every Nigerian who votes is equipped to make that vote count — and defend it.

"The 2027 elections will not be decided by politicians alone. They will be decided by citizens who showed up — and by those who didn't."

Your Vote. Your PVC. Your Responsibility.

The 2027 general elections are now fixed for 16 January 2027 (Presidential & National Assembly) and 6 February 2027 (Governorship & State Assembly), under INEC's revised timetable issued in February 2026. INEC's Continuous Voter Registration (CVR) exercise provides rolling opportunities for new registrations and transfers. If you are not yet registered — or if you are registered but have not collected your Permanent Voter Card — the window is still open. But windows close.

Nigeria's history is littered with the consequences of citizen disengagement: elections decided by narrow margins while millions of eligible voters stayed home; mandates claimed by those who showed up while those with the most to lose calculated that their single vote would not matter. It will matter in 2027. It will matter in aggregate. And the aggregate is made up of individual decisions — yours, and your neighbour's, and your colleague's — made weeks or months before election day, when the quiet act of registering and collecting a card either happens or does not.

Do not outsource your democracy to those with more money and less conscience. Register. Collect your PVC. Know your polling unit. Show up.

2027 ELECTION READINESS — WHAT YOU MUST DO NOW

1. Register to vote — If you are 18 or older and not yet registered, visit the nearest INEC office or check inecnigeria.org for CVR dates and locations in your state.

2. Collect your PVC — Registration without collection is registration without power. Return to the INEC office where you registered and collect your Permanent Voter Card. Bring valid ID.

3. Confirm your polling unit — Use INEC's Voter Status Verification System at voters.inecnigeria.org (or cvr.inecnigeria.org/vvs) to verify your registration status and confirm your assigned polling unit.

4. Mobilise your community — Every uncollected PVC in your household, your workplace, or your street is a vote that does not exist. Make this your personal civic project before 2027.

5. Stay informed — Return to NITIZEN for election-readiness guides, your rights on election day, how to report irregularities through See-gnal RedFlag, and AskNaija for any specific civic question you need answered.

  • [³]Human Rights Watch, "Nigeria: Democratic Transition in Jeopardy" (1993). Nwosu, Humphrey. "Laying the Foundation for Nigeria's Democracy" (2008) — the NEC chairman's account of June 12. Legislature · Accountability · Conscience Letters No. 002

The Legislature We Deserve: On Nigeria's National Assembly Budget and Its Accountability Deficit

NITIZEN EDITORIAL · MAY 2026 · 5 MIN READ

National Assembly · Budget Reality Check · 2025
₦344.85B
NASS Statutory Transfer
₦6.93T
Projects Inserted (BudgIT)
469
Legislators Funded
Avg. Teacher Salary (monthly)₦30,000
NASS Budget (÷ 12 months)₦28.7B/mo
Source: Budget Office of the Federation 2025 · BudgIT Budget Analysis Feb 2025

In a country where a public school teacher earns approximately ₦30,000 a month — often paid late, sometimes not at all — the Nigerian National Assembly received a statutory transfer of ₦344.85 billion in the 2025 Appropriation Act[¹] Verified, in addition to an extra ₦170 billion allocation captured under the Service Wide Vote[¹]. This covers the running costs of 469 legislators and their support apparatus: the staff, the vehicles, the security details, the overseas trips, the constituency allowances, and the considerable personal emoluments that make a Nigerian lawmaker one of the highest-paid in the world relative to per capita income. Beyond this, BudgIT documented that lawmakers inserted 11,122 additional projects worth ₦6.93 trillion into the 2025 budget[²] Verified — a figure that dwarfs the statutory allocation itself.

Let us sit with that ratio for a moment. Nigeria's GDP per capita is approximately $2,000[³] (World Bank, 2023). Its legislators earn, in allowances alone, multiples of what the average Nigerian earns in a lifetime. The legislature that is constitutionally mandated to represent the people has, over time, become an institution that is sustained by the people but oriented primarily toward itself.

"A parliament that costs more than it produces — in legislation, in oversight, in service — is not a parliament. It is a welfare scheme for the politically connected."

The Oversight Paradox

The National Assembly's constitutional role is threefold: legislation, representation, and oversight. Of these three, it is in oversight that the legislature's failure is most consequential and most visible. The executive has, in successive administrations, expanded its reach — spending without appropriation, deploying security forces without legislative authorisation, and managing state resources with opacity that would be challenged in any functioning democracy.

Nigeria's National Assembly, with rare exceptions, has watched this happen. It has held few meaningful investigative hearings that resulted in accountability. It has passed few consequential anti-corruption or institutional reform bills from its own initiative. Its relationship with the executive has too often resembled partnership rather than oversight — understandable given party dynamics, but constitutionally indefensible.

What a Legislature Should Cost — and Deliver

The question is not whether a legislature requires adequate funding. It does. Lawmaking, constituency service, and effective oversight require resources. The question is proportionality: whether the cost of the institution bears any reasonable relationship to what it delivers for the citizens who fund it.

By that measure, Nigeria's National Assembly is not delivering. The ratio of legislative output to legislative expenditure — measured not merely in bills passed but in laws that demonstrably improved Nigerian lives — is deeply unfavourable. And until Nigerian citizens begin to demand otherwise — to track legislative performance, to know how their representatives vote, to show up at constituency offices and demand accountability — the legislature will continue to be exactly as expensive and exactly as unproductive as it has always been.

This is what Conscience Letters is for. Not outrage — outrage is easy and cheap. Analysis is harder. And action — informed, sustained, civic action — is what actually changes things.

References & Sources
  • [¹]Federal Republic of Nigeria, Appropriation Act 2025. Budget Office of the Federation — "2025 Budget Summary," January 2025. National Assembly statutory transfer: ₦344.85 billion. Service Wide Vote supplementary allocation corroborated by BudgIT and Premium Times budget analysis, January 2025. budgetoffice.gov.ng
  • [²]BudgIT, "Analysis of the 2025 Appropriation Act," February 2025. 11,122 constituency projects totalling ₦6.93 trillion documented across NASS insertions. Full dataset: budgit.ng. Independently corroborated by Punch ("NASS Inflates Budget," February 2025) and The Continent.
  • [³]World Bank, "GDP per capita (current US$) — Nigeria," World Development Indicators 2023. Figure: $2,085. data.worldbank.org/indicator/NY.GDP.PCAP.CD?locations=NG

NTZ·CL·003 — Conscience Letters · Electoral Democracy · NITIZEN Editorial · June 2026
Electoral Democracy · Institutional Failure · Conscience Letters No. 003

The Broken Machine: INEC, Institutional Failure, and the Risk of Repeating 2023 in 2027

NITIZEN EDITORIAL · JUNE 2026 · 16 MIN READ

There is a particular kind of institutional failure that does not announce itself with a single dramatic collapse. It accumulates — in procurement decisions never scrutinised, in legal ambiguities never resolved, in accountability mechanisms never enforced, in transparency promises never fulfilled. Nigeria’s Independent National Electoral Commission delivered precisely this kind of failure in 2023. The question that should preoccupy every Nigerian who cares about the republic is not whether that failure occurred. It is whether the machine has been fixed — or whether, with 2027 approaching, it is still broken in all the same places.

This analysis does not relitigate who won or lost in 2023. The courts have spoken on that question, and the legitimacy of their rulings is a separate debate. What concerns us here is the architecture of malfunction: the specific points at which the system failed to protect the integrity of the vote, the institutional and legal conditions that made those failures possible, and the concrete reforms that must be implemented before the next general election. Without them, the 2023 crisis is not an aberration. It is a rehearsal.

“A broken machine does not know it is broken. It keeps running — producing outputs that look like results, following procedures that look like process — until someone measures what came out against what should have. Nigeria’s electoral machine has been measured. The reading is not good.”

Transparency Gaps: When Openness Is Promised but Not Delivered

The 2023 general elections were, by INEC’s own advance communications, supposed to represent a new standard of transparency. The commission made specific, public commitments: real-time upload of polling unit results to the INEC Result Viewing Portal (IReV), biometric accreditation through BVAS that would generate an auditable voter trail, and a collation process that would be observable at every tier. These were not vague aspirations. They were operational promises against which INEC’s performance could and should be measured.

What emerged on and after February 25, 2023, was a systematic transparency deficit. IReV uploads stalled during the most critical post-poll window. When results eventually appeared, portal data was incomplete, and in multiple states the figures bore no consistent relationship to declared collated results. Verified[¹] INEC's response was blanket statements about "technical difficulties" — never followed by a forensic post-mortem. Three years later, that post-mortem still does not exist publicly. INEC has not specified what failed on IReV — server capacity, bandwidth, field non-compliance, or software. No independent body can therefore verify whether the conditions that produced the 2023 failure have been remedied. Transparency about transparency failures is the minimum standard. INEC has not met it.

BVAS: Accountability for a System That Was Never Fully Audited

The Bimodal Voter Accreditation System represented a genuine and significant advancement in Nigeria’s electoral technology. By linking biometric authentication to digital result transmission, it was designed to close two of the widest fraud pathways in the country’s electoral history: ghost voter accreditation and the disconnection between polling unit counts and declared results. In states and polling units where BVAS functioned as designed, the system delivered on its promise. The problem is that it did not function as designed across enough of the country to constitute a credible national deployment.

Device malfunctions in Lagos, Kano, Rivers, and several other states were documented not by opposition parties alone but by the EU Election Observation Mission, by YIAGA Africa’s Parallel Vote Tabulation exercise, by the Joint International Observer Group, and by INEC’s own post-election reports. Verified[²] The malfunctions led to delayed accreditation, extended waiting times that suppressed turnout, and in some cases the outright exclusion of voters who had registered and arrived at their polling units only to find that no functioning device was available to authenticate them.

Why BVAS failed where it failed has never been independently established. The geographic distribution of malfunctions was not random — independent analyses identified a statistical concentration of failures in urban areas with high opposition support. Whether this reflects deliberate sabotage, poor procurement, or coincidence remains unresolved. INEC has published no remediation plan and commissioned no independent audit of BVAS performance. For 2027, the commission will deploy a system whose failure modes are undocumented. That is not a reformed system. It is a deferred liability.

Result Transmission Failures: The Chain That Broke

Electronic result transmission was the centrepiece of INEC’s 2023 integrity architecture. The design was sound: BVAS devices at each of Nigeria’s 176,846 polling units would scan and upload the Form EC8A immediately after counting, creating a publicly visible, timestamped record before results entered the collation chain. If this had worked consistently, it would have been structurally transformative — making large-scale falsification at collation stages visible and therefore, in principle, politically costly.

The transmission chain broke at multiple points. Upload failures were concentrated in the early hours after polls closed — precisely the window in which the absence of uploaded results created the largest information vacuum and the greatest opportunity for collation manipulation. Verified[¹] By the time results began appearing on IReV in large numbers, the collation process at many ward and local government levels was already complete. The audit trail, which should have constrained collation, instead became a post-hoc document — available for comparison with declared results but no longer capable of preventing the declaration of results that diverged from the polling unit data.

This sequencing failure is structurally critical for 2027. If INEC cannot demonstrate, through credible pre-election testing, that transmission from all polling units completes within a defined and publicly monitored post-poll window, the same vulnerability persists. Technology that arrives after manipulation has occurred does not prevent it — it documents it, at best, for those with resources to pursue the discrepancy through a system designed to exhaust them.

EC8A Overreliance and the Collation Vulnerability

The legal structure underlying Nigeria’s electoral process contains a fundamental design flaw that the Electoral Act 2022 introduced technology around but failed to resolve. Form EC8A — the physical collation sheet completed at the polling unit — remains the legally primary document in electoral proceedings. The Act’s provisions for electronic transmission are framed as complementary to, not substitutive of, the physical form. In judicial proceedings, where transmitted data and physical data conflict, the physical document has been treated by courts as authoritative.

The consequence of this legal arrangement is that the entire IReV architecture rests on a foundation it cannot legally override. An actor who can access the physical Form EC8A — or the EC8B, C, and D forms that aggregate results up through the collation chain — can, in effect, overwrite the electronic record without the electronic record having any legal power to prevent it. Verified[³] This is not a theoretical vulnerability. In 2023, discrepancies between uploaded polling unit data and collated results were documented across multiple states. The electronic record showed one figure; the physical form used in the collation showed another. The physical form prevailed.

Each transfer point in the collation chain — polling unit to ward, ward to LGA, LGA to state, state to national — is a manipulation window. In 2023, result sheets arrived at collation centres already pre-completed; forms went missing and were replaced; collation officers refused to acknowledge party agents' polling unit figures. In a system where paper beats pixels, every such incident advantages the actor with physical custody of the form — which is, by design, INEC's own staff.

Political Interference and the Ecosystem of Compromise

INEC does not fail in isolation. It fails within a political ecosystem whose actors have spent decades learning how to convert every stage of the electoral process into an instrument of predetermined outcome. Understanding this ecosystem is essential to understanding why technological solutions alone cannot produce electoral integrity — and why structural and institutional reforms are the only durable remedy.

At the state level, governors represent the most powerful single node of interference. In states where a sitting governor has a direct stake in a senatorial, gubernatorial, or presidential outcome, the full apparatus of state power — state-employed civil servants, local government chairmen, state-controlled transport, security liaison officers — has historically been mobilised to shape the process. This mobilisation does not primarily take the form of ballot-stuffing on polling day, though that occurs too. It takes the form of controlling who is recruited as ad hoc electoral staff, which areas receive functioning BVAS devices and which do not, which collation centres are accessible to opposition party agents, and which security deployments are designed to facilitate voting and which are designed to suppress it.

The 2023 governorship elections in Imo, Kogi, and Bayelsa documented this ecosystem in vivid detail. Declared results diverged so pronouncedly from observable ground reality that international observers and diplomatic missions publicly questioned the process. Verified[´] In Imo, a governor removed by tribunal was reinstated by the Supreme Court in legally contested circumstances. In Kogi and Bayelsa, incumbents were declared victorious in elections multiple credible observers called neither free nor fair. The pattern reflects a model in which outcome is determined by the power resources of contestants — not the preferences of voters. For 2027, federal incumbency makes this ecosystem materially more potent: executive access to INEC's appointment structures, security deployments, and operational budget represents leverage no structural safeguard currently constrains.

Institutional Compromise: The Appointment Problem and What It Produces

Any serious analysis of INEC’s institutional failures must confront the root cause that structural reformers have identified and that successive administrations have refused to address: the commission’s leadership is appointed by the very executive whose elections it must adjudicate.

The Constitution provides for the President to nominate INEC’s chairman and national commissioners, subject to Senate confirmation. In jurisdictions where the presidency and Senate majority share a party affiliation — as has been the case for extended periods in Nigeria’s Fourth Republic — Senate confirmation is not an adversarial check. It is a ratification ceremony. The result is an institution whose most senior leadership owes its position to the executive that nominated it, operates on a budget that the executive controls, and exercises discretion over a process in which the executive has the highest possible stake. Verified[µ]

This structural dependency shapes behaviour in ways both explicit and invisible. One need not allege that INEC's chairman received direct instructions from the Presidency in 2023. It is sufficient to observe that an institution whose existence, funding, and leadership derive from a single political actor cannot be structurally independent of that actor. The bias is baked in — not because individuals are dishonest, but because the institution is constitutionally designed without independence. Nigeria's INEC is structurally compromised, and that compromise predates and postdates every individual who has served within it.

Legal Ambiguities: The Loopholes That Must Be Closed

The Electoral Act 2022 was, by the standards of Nigerian electoral legislation, a serious reform effort. Its provisions for BVAS accreditation, result transmission, and expanded grounds for election petitions represented legislative progress that should be acknowledged. But genuine reform can coexist with dangerous ambiguity — and the Act contains several provisions whose vagueness created exploitable space in 2023 and will do so again in 2027 unless addressed.

The most consequential ambiguity is the undefined standard of "substantial compliance" — the principle that an election is valid if substantially, not perfectly, compliant with legal requirements. Courts have applied it with such inconsistency that it now functions as judicial discretion so broad as to be unpredictable; tribunals in different states applied it to opposite effect in factually similar 2023 circumstances. The Act does not define substantial compliance for a BVAS/IReV election: what percentage of polling units must have uploaded results, what BVAS malfunction means for unit validity, or how electronic-physical discrepancies affect legal outcome. That ambiguity is a structural gift to whoever controls physical documentation. Verified[³]

A second critical ambiguity concerns campaign finance. The Electoral Act sets spending ceilings that are routinely exceeded by every major candidate — in some cases by orders of magnitude — without consequence. INEC’s campaign finance monitoring function lacks audit powers, prosecutorial independence, and the resources necessary to investigate violations. The result is that campaign finance regulation exists as text in a statute and nowhere else. Verified[³] In an election cycle where money determines mobilisation, access, and ultimately votes, the absence of credible spending regulation is not a procedural gap. It is a structural advantage for candidates with the largest war chests — and a structural disadvantage for every other participant and for democracy itself.

Accountability Breakdowns: The Officials Who Faced No Consequences

The post-2023 accountability record is not merely disappointing. It is, on the available evidence, close to non-existent. INEC arraigned a number of presiding and returning officers for alleged result manipulation in the months following the elections. The prosecutions were conducted through the regular federal court system, without dedicated electoral crime jurisdiction, without specialised forensic capacity, and without the institutional insulation from political pressure that effective prosecution of politically sensitive offences requires. As of mid-2026, the vast majority of those prosecutions have stalled, collapsed, or produced acquittals. Verified[¶] No senior electoral official has been convicted and sentenced for offences relating to the 2023 elections.

The Electoral Offences Commission — a dedicated independent prosecutorial body proposed by virtually every credible reform initiative over two decades — remains unestablished. The bill has been introduced in successive National Assembly sessions and never passed. The political calculus is not mysterious: the actors most likely to be prosecuted by such a body are overwhelmingly represented among the legislators who would need to enact it. Until electoral manipulation carries a credible risk of prosecution — swift, credible, and dissuasive — the rational choice for every official under political pressure will be the same choice made in 2023. The machine that produces impunity is still running.

Judicial Architecture: When the Court of Last Resort Leaves Citizens Unresorted

When citizens and candidates cannot trust INEC, they are directed to the judiciary. This is constitutionally correct. What the constitution does not guarantee is that the judicial process will be accessible, affordable, consistent, or timely enough to provide a genuine remedy rather than a ceremonial one.

Electoral litigation in Nigeria structurally disadvantages petitioners at every tier. Certified true copies of results must be obtained from an INEC with institutional incentives to delay. Technical evidence on BVAS and IReV must be adduced from systems whose architecture INEC has never been required to disclose. All of this must complete within 180 days for presidential petitions — timelines that systematically favour the institutional status quo. The 2023 petition process further revealed judicial inconsistency: in at least four states, tribunal findings were reversed on appeal not on new facts but on different applications of the same legal standards. Verified[·] The doctrine applied to one petitioner in one state produced a different outcome than the same doctrine applied to a materially similar petitioner in another. That is not a judiciary working through novel territory. It is one whose electoral jurisprudence is insufficiently principled — and susceptible to influences that have no place in adjudication.

Media, Disinformation, and the Information Ecosystem of Elections

The integrity of a modern election is not determined solely by what happens at the polling unit or the collation centre. It is also determined by what citizens believe is happening — and what they believe they can do about it. In 2023, the information ecosystem surrounding the election was compromised by the deliberate production and rapid dissemination of false narratives at every stage of the process.

Fabricated result sheets circulated on WhatsApp before any official results were announced. False claims about candidate eligibility, polling unit closures, and security incidents spread faster than corrections. Coordinated influence operations amplified misleading content in ways that suppressed turnout in targeted areas. Verified[¸] Nigeria's regulatory architecture for electoral information integrity is essentially absent: the NBC has no operational framework for requiring correction of electoral misinformation; major digital platforms face negligible accountability to Nigerian authorities. By 2027, with AI-assisted content generation making disinformation campaigns cheaper and more convincing to produce, this gap represents one of the most significant threats to electoral credibility Nigeria has yet faced.

A Blueprint for Restoration: What Must Change Before 2027

Identifying failure is the easier part of this analysis. What matters for the republic’s future is whether diagnosis can be converted into reform — and whether the political will and civic pressure necessary to drive reform can be assembled before the window closes. What follows is not a comprehensive wish list but the minimum set of interventions without which 2027 will almost certainly reproduce 2023’s credibility deficit.

Political reform: INEC appointment and funding independence. A constitutional amendment must establish an independent selection panel — judiciary, bar, civil society, academia — to nominate INEC's chairman and commissioners, with the executive's role limited to formal appointment from that shortlist. INEC's budget must be constitutionally designated as a first-line charge on the Consolidated Revenue Fund, removing executive discretion over its release. Neither reform is logistically difficult. Both require a political class willing to constrain its own leverage. That willingness must be demanded by citizens — with specific legislative targets.

Legal reform: electronic equivalence, defined standards, campaign finance. The Electoral Act must be amended before 2027 to grant electronic result transmission data legal equivalence with physical collation forms, subject to cryptographically verified chain of custody. Where transmitted and physical data conflict, an automatic independent technical audit — not judicial discretion — must be the mandatory first response. Substantial compliance must be operationally defined in statute: what percentage of failed accreditations or missing uploads triggers an automatic result review? These are political decisions dressed as technical ones — and until legislated, they will be decided differently every time. On campaign finance: an independent audit body with powers to inspect party accounts and levy meaningful sanctions must replace the current fiction of INEC-administered spending limits.

Civic reform: electoral literacy and citizen documentation. Structured electoral literacy programmes — covering accreditation, rights on election day, collation observation, and irregularity reporting — must reach every local government in all major languages before 2027. Civic readiness is not only INEC's responsibility; it belongs to every organisation, journalist, and citizen who understands what is at stake. NITIZEN's See-gnal initiative — RedFlag for real-time irregularity reporting, The Ledger for institutional tracking — exists to give citizens the infrastructure to document what they witness. The collation process is most vulnerable where citizens are absent. The most powerful deterrent to manipulation is not technology. It is witnesses.

Technological reform: independent audit and transmission integrity. INEC must commission and publish an independent audit of BVAS and IReV performance across 2023 — conducted by a consortium of international election technology specialists, Nigerian cybersecurity professionals, and civil society observers — with findings published in full and a verifiable remediation plan. For 2027, BVAS deployment must include a publicly specified backup protocol for device failures, replacing the discretion that created manipulation space in 2023. Result transmission must be end-to-end encrypted with hash verification that any technical observer can independently check — making tampering mathematically detectable rather than merely alleged.

Institutional reform: Electoral Offences Commission and judicial standardisation. The Electoral Offences Commission Bill must be passed and in force before the 2027 cycle opens. Without dedicated prosecutorial capacity, electoral crime remains cost-free for those most able to benefit from it. The National Judicial Council must simultaneously publish standardised guidelines for electoral cases — covering electronic evidence treatment, the definition of substantial compliance in a technology-enabled election, IReV evidentiary weight, and petitioners' document rights — before 2027 litigation begins. Guidelines developed during litigation are not guidelines. They are retroactive rationalisations.

Media reform: electoral information integrity framework. The NBC and Nigerian Press Council must develop, before 2027, a framework requiring major broadcast outlets to correct demonstrably false electoral claims within defined timeframes, prohibiting electoral advertising from anonymous funders, and establishing a rapid-response verification mechanism. Digital platforms operating in Nigeria must be required — through regulation where necessary — to provide real-time disclosure of political advertising spend, remove content identified as false by a defined multi-stakeholder body, and give Nigerian civil society organisations the same transparency tools available to researchers in other jurisdictions.

The Calculus of Trust: What Restoration Actually Requires

Public trust in an electoral system is not restored by assurance. It is restored by evidence — by the observable fulfilment of specific commitments, by the demonstrable punishment of specific violations, and by the structural reform of the conditions that made violations possible in the first place. Nigeria has, since 2023, received assurances in abundance. It has not received evidence.

INEC has spoken of technology improvements without publishing specifications or commissioning verification. The National Assembly has held electoral reform hearings without producing legislation. The President has spoken of commitment to a free and fair 2027 election without supporting a single structural reform that would constrain his administration's leverage over the process. The gap between stated institutional intentions and the structural conditions of the electoral system has not narrowed since 2023. It has, if anything, widened.

What trust restoration requires is not goodwill. It requires that INEC be structurally unable to be captured — not just that its current leadership chooses to resist capture. It requires that electoral manipulation carry a credible risk of prosecution — not just that INEC occasionally arraigns officials who will be acquitted two years later. It requires that the legal framework give citizens and petitioners genuine tools to challenge results — not just the right to file petitions in a system designed to exhaust them. And it requires that citizens be equipped, informed, and present — not passive recipients of whatever result is declared, but active participants in every stage of the process that produces it.

The 2027 election is not yet inevitable. Its outcome is not predetermined. But the conditions that determine its credibility are being set now — in every legislative session that passes without electoral reform, in every audit that is not commissioned, in every prosecution that is not pursued. The machine is still broken. The time available to fix it is measurable in months, not years. The citizens who refuse to accept another 2023 are the only constituency with both the interest and the power to demand that it be fixed.

NITIZEN will track every dimension of this story — every reform tabled, every accountability failure documented, every civic action taken — between now and the January–February 2027 polls. This is what the platform is for.

Two layers. One standard.

Verified Knowledge Base

66 pre-written, fact-checked, sourced answers covering 16 civic categories. Responses are delivered instantly — zero API latency, zero hallucination. Every answer is attributed to its source legislation, government data, or official report.

Data Privacy — NDPC Compliance

Your Privacy on NITIZEN

What We Collect

Only data you voluntarily submit through forms. AskNaija KB responses require no API call — nothing leaves your browser. AI-mode queries are transmitted to Anthropic's API to generate your response and are not stored by NITIZEN.

AskNaija & Anthropic

KB-matched questions are answered entirely in your browser. AI-mode questions are sent to the Anthropic API. NITIZEN does not log or retain your questions. Anthropic's API terms prohibit training on API inputs.

Your Rights (NDPA 2023)

Right to access, correct, delete, and port your data. Submit any request to hello@nitizen.ng with subject "Data Rights Request" — we respond within 7 days. Complaints: ndpc.gov.ng

🔫 Police Brutality · Delta State · Effurun
Active — Prosecution Pending
Extrajudicial Killing of Mene Ogidi, 28 — April 26, 2026 · Case #RF-001-2026 Verified

Mene Ogidi, a 28-year-old Nigerian, was shot at close range by ASP Nuhu Usman of the Nigeria Police Force at the Benin Motor Park along the Warri–Sapele Expressway, Effurun, Delta State. A widely circulated video showed Ogidi seated on the ground with his hands tied behind his back before being shot by an officer in plain clothes. He had left home to collect a waybill on behalf of a friend in Sapele and never returned alive. His family disclosed that police had previously killed his younger brother in a separate incident. The Force Disciplinary Committee found ASP Usman acted "in gross violation of Force Order 237 and other extant regulations governing the use of firearms," describing his conduct as "unlawful, unprofessional, and a clear betrayal of the oath to protect life."[¹] Inspector-General of Police Tunji Disu approved Usman's immediate dismissal, forwarded for ratification by the Police Service Commission. Verified[²] Delta State Governor Sheriff Oborevwori described the killing as "unwarranted, unprovoked and barbaric." Verified The National Human Rights Commission and the Police Service Commission both issued formal condemnations. Criminal prosecution proceedings are underway.

Filed: May 2026 · Effurun, Delta State · Officer: ASP Nuhu Usman (Dismissed) · Status: Criminal prosecution pending · Sources: IGP statement, PSC statement, NHRC statement, BBC Pidgin, Pulse Nigeria
🏫 School Attack · Oyo State · Oriire LGA
Active — Children Missing · Teacher Killed
Oyo School Attack: 46 Abducted, Teacher Beheaded — May 15–16, 2026 · Case #RF-004-2026 Documented

On the night of May 15–16, 2026, armed bandits attacked three schools in Oriire Local Government Area, Oyo State — abducting 7 teachers and 39 pupils. Mathematics teacher Michael Oyedokun was subsequently beheaded. The attacks represent one of the most significant school abduction incidents in southwestern Nigeria since the northeast-focused Chibok (2014) and Kankara (2020) mass kidnappings, marking a dangerous southward expansion of school-targeting banditry. Documented Oyo State Governor Seyi Makinde confirmed the crisis and deployed joint security forces. The Nigerian Army, Police, and DSS launched a rescue operation. As of NITIZEN's filing date, the fate of the remaining abductees was unconfirmed. NITIZEN calls on the Federal Government and Oyo State to: (1) provide a transparent public update on all 46 abductees; (2) deploy all available intelligence and recovery assets without delay; (3) ensure full accountability for the attack — including investigation of any security failures that enabled it; and (4) implement immediate hardening of school perimeters in at-risk LGAs across the southwest.

Filed: May 2026 · Oriire LGA, Oyo State · Victims: 7 teachers, 39 pupils abducted; 1 teacher (Michael Oyedokun) killed · Status: Rescue operation ongoing · Sources: Oyo State Government, Nigerian Army statement, BBC Pidgin, Channels Television, The Punch, Vanguard
💸 Corruption · Federal Level
Tracking
Ghost Workers & Payroll Irregularities in the Federal Civil Service · Case #RF-002-2026

Nigeria's Integrated Personnel and Payroll Information System (IPPIS) was introduced to eliminate ghost workers from the federal payroll. The Auditor-General's 2023 report flagged billions in questionable payroll entries across multiple Ministries, Departments and Agencies.[³] The National Assembly's Public Accounts Committee has repeatedly recommended forensic audits of payroll records. Accountability outcomes — including prosecutions and funds recovery — remain incomplete. See-gnal is tracking disclosures, audit reports, and prosecution updates.

Filed: May 2026 · Scope: Federal MDAs · Status: Audits ongoing — prosecutorial action pending
🏛️ Bad Governance · Lagos State
Documented
Waterfront Community Demolitions Without Statutory Compensation · Case #RF-003-2026

Between 2023 and 2025, Lagos State government carried out demolitions of waterfront communities with affected residents reporting absence of prior notice, resettlement alternatives, or compensation as required under the Lagos State Urban and Regional Planning and Development Law[⁴] and the constitutional right to shelter. Verified Human rights organisations documented the displacements. See-gnal calls on Lagos State to publish a complete resettlement and compensation record, as mandated by law.

Filed: May 2026 · Lagos State · Status: Documented — Advocacy ongoing

✍️ Civic Essay NTZ·SG·OM·001
The Death of Mene Ogidi Is Not an Isolated Incident. It Is a System.

When the video of Mene Ogidi's killing circulated in late April 2026, Nigerians reacted with horror. They were right to. But horror alone is not enough. ASP Nuhu Usman did not invent impunity — he inherited it. The Nigeria Police Force has for decades operated within a culture in which extrajudicial violence carries no consistent institutional consequence. #EndSARS was a cry for reform in 2020. Verified Government panels were set up. Reports were written. Mene Ogidi is buried. The officer has been dismissed — but dismissed is not convicted. And conviction without systemic reform is not change. It is performance. Nigeria does not have a bad officer problem. It has a structural impunity problem. Until the institution changes, the individuals will not.

NationalNITIZEN OpenMic · May 2026
👁️ Community Report NTZ·SG·OM·002
Our Local Government Has Not Held a Town Hall in Three Years — Oyo State

Lagelu Local Government Area has not convened a public town hall in over three years. Residents have no structured channel to engage elected officials. Constituency projects are invisible. Budget allocations are announced without community input. This is what democratic failure looks like at the grassroots — not dramatic, not viral, just the slow erosion of accountability in places the cameras never reach.

Oyo StateCommunity Observer · May 2026
📢 Policy Analysis NTZ·SG·OM·003
The National Tax Acts 2025: Reform or Burden? What Every Nigerian Needs to Know

The Nigeria Tax Act 2025 and the Nigeria Tax Administration Act 2025 — signed into law in mid-2025 Verified — represent the most comprehensive reform of Nigeria's tax framework in decades. For the formal sector, they rationalise multiple levies into a single-window compliance framework. For the informal sector — traders, artisans, market women who constitute over 90% of employment — the picture is more complex: expanded compliance obligations that presuppose access to banking and digital infrastructure that millions lack. The reform is directionally necessary. Its equity in implementation is the test Nigeria cannot afford to fail.

FederalCivic Analyst · May 2026
🏥 Personal Testimony NTZ·SG·OM·004
I Was Charged ₦92,000 at a Public Hospital for Treatment the BHCPF Was Supposed to Cover

The Basic Healthcare Provision Fund exists, by law, to ensure that primary healthcare is accessible to Nigerians who cannot afford private care. In April 2026, I presented at a federal government secondary health facility in Abuja and was charged ₦92,000 for treatment. When I asked the billing officer about BHCPF coverage, she said: "The drugs are not available. You have to buy them outside." This is not an accident. It is the predictable outcome of chronic underfunding, supply chain collapse, and institutional indifference. The law exists. The infrastructure does not.

Abuja FCTAnonymous · May 2026
🌧️ Infrastructure Report NTZ·SG·OM·005
This Federal Road Has Been "Under Rehabilitation" for Nine Years

A major highway segment in Anambra State has been flagged as "under rehabilitation" since at least 2016. Multiple contracts have been awarded; mobilisation fees disbursed; contractors sighted briefly, then absent for months at a time. The road remains dangerous. Fatal accidents are documented on this corridor every month. The Bureau of Public Procurement records show at least three separate contract awards on this route. Verified Where the cumulative expenditure went remains publicly unexplained. See-gnal is preparing a Freedom of Information request to the Federal Ministry of Works.

Anambra StateResident Correspondent · May 2026

Home/See-gnal/Critika/Featured Critique
✍️ Written Critique · Critika Featured Piece

Buhari Promised Security.
Here Is the Record.

NITIZEN EDITORIAL · MAY 2026 · 10 MIN READ

In 2015, Muhammadu Buhari campaigned on a single, clarion promise above all others: security. The Goodluck Jonathan administration, his campaign argued, had failed Nigerians in the most fundamental duty of the state — the protection of lives and territory. Boko Haram had seized swathes of the northeast. Kidnappings had become routine. Farmers and herders were clashing across the Middle Belt in conflicts that left thousands dead. Nigeria, the argument went, needed a general — a man of iron discipline who understood security from the inside.

Nigerians, millions of them, believed this argument. Buhari won decisively. He served two terms — 2015 to 2023. What follows is not an opinion. It is a record.

The Promises, Measured

The PromiseThe RecordVerdict
"We will defeat Boko Haram technically within months" Boko Haram and ISWAP remained operationally active at end of tenure; thousands of military personnel killed; large areas of the northeast remained under threat ⚠ Broken
"Kidnapping will be brought under control" School kidnappings escalated — Chibok (2014, pre-Buhari but unresolved), Kankara (2020), Kagara (2021), Tegina (2021). Bandits openly demanded and received ransoms ⚠ Broken
"Farmer-herder conflicts will be resolved" Deaths from farmer-herder clashes exceeded 7,000 between 2016 and 2022 by multiple estimates. No structured resolution framework was implemented ⚠ Broken
"Banditry will be crushed" Banditry expanded from northwestern states to become a national security crisis. The government at points engaged bandits in dialogue rather than military prosecution ⚠ Broken
"Security forces will be properly equipped and motivated" Partial improvement in equipment; families of fallen troops protested unpaid death benefits; reports of soldiers abandoning positions due to morale failures ◑ Partial
"The military will not interfere in political processes" No military coup or direct military interference in civilian governance occurred during the Buhari years ✓ Kept

The Counting of the Dead

Statistics are cold. Behind each number is a name, a family, a community shattered. But numbers are what governance must ultimately answer to — because governance is a promise made at scale. The Armed Conflict Location and Event Data Project (ACLED) documented tens of thousands of conflict-related deaths in Nigeria during the Buhari years. The Internal Displacement Monitoring Centre estimated that Nigeria had over 3.6 million internally displaced persons by 2022 — one of the largest displaced populations in Africa.

These figures do not prove that a different administration would have performed better. Security challenges of this complexity are not solved by political will alone. What they do prove is this: the promise was made, the promise was specific, and the promise was not kept. In a functioning democracy, that matters. Citizens deserve to know.

"The purpose of Critika is not vengeance against past administrations. It is the cultivation of a civic reflex — the habit of measuring governance against its own words, and demanding answers for the distance between them."

Why This Matters for 2027

We review the Buhari security record not to relitigate the past but to equip Nigerians for the future. Every candidate who contests in 2027 will make promises — on security, on the economy, on electricity, on education, on corruption. Nigerian citizens who have learned to hold past promises against present performance will be better equipped to evaluate those new promises critically rather than emotionally.

That is the work of Critika. Not rage — rigour. Not complaint — evidence. Not silence — art, data, and the refusal to forget what was said. Every government makes promises. Every promise leaves a record. And every citizen has both the right and the responsibility to read that record clearly.

This is civic accountability. This is Critika.

This critique is open-source. Share it, build on it, respond to it. Submit your own critique at nitizen/senal#critika or email hello@nitizen.ng. We welcome counter-analyses grounded in evidence.

About the Fellowship

Not an internship.
A formation.

The NITIZEN Leadership Fellowship is a six-month immersive programme that transforms talented young Nigerians into formidable civic actors — researchers, writers, advocates, strategists, and institution-builders working at the intersection of democracy, governance, and public accountability.

01
Frontline Civic Leadership
Fellows don't observe the work — they do it. From day one, you contribute to live research, published reporting, public advocacy, and strategic projects that reach millions of Nigerians.
02
Political Education at Depth
Structured learning in constitutional law, Nigerian political economy, democratic theory, electoral systems, and comparative governance — curated for an era demanding intellectual rigour.
03
Accountability Journalism
Learn and practise the discipline of verified, evidence-based civic reporting. Fellows contribute to NITIZEN's Conscience Letters, public briefings, and accountability campaigns.
04
Full Membership Pathway
Completion of the fellowship leads directly to full NITIZEN membership — placing you within Nigeria's most rigorous civic intelligence network for the rest of your career.
Five Pillars of Work

What Fellows actually do.

🔎
Political Education & Research
Deep-dive policy analysis, parliamentary tracking, governance research, and fact-based political education for public consumption.
📋
Accountability Reporting
Verified documentation of government performance, public expenditure tracking, institutional audit, and evidence-based critique.
🗳️
Democratic Participation
Voter education, electoral integrity work, civic rights documentation, and engagement with democratic institutions at all levels.
📢
Civic Advocacy
Designing and executing campaigns that shift public consciousness, build coalitions, and demand policy accountability from elected officials.
🌍
Public Engagement
Building and nurturing NITIZEN's stakeholder community — from grassroots outreach to institutional partnerships and media relations.
Who Should Apply

This fellowship was built
for people like you.

AGE
30 years old or younger. We are investing in Nigeria's next thirty years, and we want the people who will live them.
MIND
Intellectually driven. You read widely. You think carefully. You are not satisfied with surface-level narratives about Nigeria's challenges.
ETHOS
Civic-minded. You believe governance matters. You're not cynical enough to walk away, and not naive enough to think change comes without organised, informed effort.
FOCUS
Deeply interested in governance, democracy, and nation-building — in theory, in practice, and in the uncomfortable gap between the two.
COMMITMENT
Able to commit 10–12 hours per week across a six-month period. Fellows are contributors, not spectators. The work is real.
SKILL
You bring at least one competency: research, writing, design, data analysis, video, community organising, strategy, communications, or operations.

Fellowship Tracks

Eight ways to contribute.

Fellows are placed across eight functional tracks aligned with NITIZEN's operational mission. Every track is a discipline. Every fellow is a practitioner.

Track 01
Research & Intelligence
Policy research, data gathering, source verification, and the production of NITIZEN's core analytical content. Rigorous. Evidence-first. Published.
Track 02
Writing & Editorial
Essays, briefings, Conscience Letters, campaign copy, and long-form civic journalism. For those who believe words are instruments of change.
Track 03
Design & Visual Communication
Campaign graphics, infographics, data visualisation, and brand execution that translate complex governance issues into public-facing power.
Track 04
Advocacy & Campaigns
Strategic campaign development, coalition building, petition drives, and the organised public pressure that moves institutions.
Track 05
Community Engagement
Grassroots outreach, stakeholder relations, community listening, and the human infrastructure that makes civic movements real.
Track 06
Strategy & Policy
Organisational strategy, policy positioning, scenario planning, and the systems-level thinking that keeps NITIZEN ahead of the moment.
Track 07
Digital & Social Media
Platform content, audience growth, social intelligence, digital campaigning, and NITIZEN's public digital presence.
Track 08
Operations & Support
Project coordination, programme execution, administrative excellence, and the operational backbone that makes everything else possible.
